prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We show that the globular cluster mass function (GCMF) in the Milky Way depends on cluster half-mass density (rho_h) in the sense that the turnover mass M_TO increases with rho_h while the width of the GCMF decreases. We argue that this is the expected signature of the slow erosion of a mass function that initially rose towards low masses, predominantly through cluster evaporation driven by internal two-body relaxation. We find excellent agreement between the observed GCMF -- including its dependence on internal density rho_h, central concentration c, and Galactocentric distance r_gc -- and a simple model in which the relaxation-driven mass-loss rates of clusters are approximated by -dM/dt = mu_ev ~ rho_h^{1/2}. In particular, we recover the well-known insensitivity of M_TO to r_gc. This feature does not derive from a literal ``universality'' of the GCMF turnover mass, but rather from a significant variation of M_TO with rho_h -- the expected outcome of relaxation-driven cluster disruption -- plus significant scatter in rho_h as a function of r_gc. Our conclusions are the same if the evaporation rates are assumed to depend instead on the mean volume or surface densities of clusters inside their tidal radii, as mu_ev ~ rho_t^{1/2} or mu_ev ~ Sigma_t^{3/4} -- alternative prescriptions that are physically motivated but involve cluster properties (rho_t and Sigma_t) that are not as well defined or as readily observable as rho_h. In all cases, the normalization of mu_ev required to fit the GCMF implies cluster lifetimes that are within the range of standard values (although falling towards the low end of this range). Our analysis does not depend on any assumptions or information about velocity anisotropy in the globular cluster system.

outputs.L1:
We show that the globular cluster mass function (GCMF) in the Milky Way depends on cluster half-mass density, \(\rho_h\), such that the turnover mass, \(M_{\rm TO}\), increases with \(\rho_h\), while the width of the GCMF decreases. We argue that this is the expected signature of the slow erosion of a mass function that initially rose toward low masses, driven predominantly by cluster evaporation due to internal two-body relaxation.

We find excellent agreement between the observed GCMF—including its dependence on internal density \(\rho_h\), central concentration \(c\), and Galactocentric distance \(r_{\rm gc}\)—and a simple model in which the relaxation-driven mass-loss rates of clusters are approximated by
\[
-\frac{dM}{dt} = \mu_{\rm ev} \sim \rho_h^{1/2}.
\]
In particular, we recover the well-known insensitivity of \(M_{\rm TO}\) to \(r_{\rm gc}\). This feature does not arise from a literal “universality” of the GCMF turnover mass, but rather from a significant variation of \(M_{\rm TO}\) with \(\rho_h\)—the expected outcome of relaxation-driven cluster disruption—combined with significant scatter in \(\rho_h\) as a function of \(r_{\rm gc}\).

Our conclusions are unchanged if the evaporation rates are instead assumed to depend on the mean volume or surface densities of clusters within their tidal radii, such that \(\mu_{\rm ev} \sim \rho_t^{1/2}\) or \(\mu_{\rm ev} \sim \Sigma_t^{3/4}\). These alternative prescriptions are physically motivated, but they involve cluster properties, \(\rho_t\) and \(\Sigma_t\), that are less well defined and less readily observable than \(\rho_h\). In all cases, the normalization of \(\mu_{\rm ev}\) required to fit the GCMF implies cluster lifetimes within the range of standard values, although toward the lower end of that range. Our analysis does not rely on any assumptions or information regarding velocity anisotropy in the globular cluster system.
outputs.L2:
We demonstrate that, in the Milky Way, the globular cluster mass function (GCMF) varies with cluster half-mass density, \(\rho_h\): the turnover mass, \(M_{\rm TO}\), becomes larger as \(\rho_h\) increases, while the GCMF becomes narrower. We interpret this as the natural imprint of the gradual depletion of an original mass function that increased toward lower masses, mainly caused by cluster evaporation due to internal two-body relaxation.

The observed GCMF is reproduced very well—including its trends with internal density \(\rho_h\), central concentration \(c\), and Galactocentric radius \(r_{\rm gc}\)—by a simple model in which relaxation-driven cluster mass-loss rates are described approximately by  
\[
-dM/dt = \mu_{\rm ev} \sim \rho_h^{1/2}.
\]
This model also recovers the familiar result that \(M_{\rm TO}\) shows little dependence on \(r_{\rm gc}\). However, this behavior is not evidence for a strictly “universal” GCMF turnover mass. Instead, it arises because \(M_{\rm TO}\) changes substantially with \(\rho_h\), as expected for cluster disruption governed by relaxation, while \(\rho_h\) itself exhibits large scatter at any given \(r_{\rm gc}\).

We reach the same conclusions if evaporation rates are taken to scale instead with clusters’ average volume density or surface density inside their tidal radii, using  
\[
\mu_{\rm ev} \sim \rho_t^{1/2}
\]
or  
\[
\mu_{\rm ev} \sim \Sigma_t^{3/4}.
\]
These alternatives are also physically motivated, though they rely on quantities—\(\rho_t\) and \(\Sigma_t\)—that are less clearly defined and less directly measured than \(\rho_h\).

For every version of the model, the normalization of \(\mu_{\rm ev}\) needed to match the GCMF corresponds to cluster lifetimes that lie within the standard accepted range, though toward its shorter-lifetime end. Our results do not rely on any assumptions or data concerning velocity anisotropy in the Galactic globular cluster system.
outputs.L3:
The mass function of Milky Way globular clusters shows a clear dependence on cluster half-mass density. In particular, the characteristic turnover mass increases as the half-mass density becomes larger, while the width of the mass function decreases. This means that denser clusters tend to have mass distributions that peak at higher masses and are more narrowly concentrated around that peak, whereas lower-density clusters retain broader mass functions with lower turnover masses.

This behavior is naturally explained if the present-day globular cluster population evolved from an initial population that contained many low-mass clusters. Over time, these lower-mass systems were gradually depleted through evaporation, a process driven primarily by internal two-body relaxation. In two-body relaxation, repeated gravitational encounters between stars redistribute energy within a cluster. Some stars gain enough energy to escape, causing the cluster to lose mass slowly over many relaxation times. Because this process is more effective in clusters with shorter relaxation times, it produces systematic changes in the mass function that depend on internal cluster density.

Observed globular cluster mass functions, including their correlations with internal density, central concentration, and Galactocentric distance, are well reproduced by models in which the relaxation-driven mass-loss rate scales with the square root of the cluster’s half-mass density. In such models, clusters with higher half-mass densities lose mass at a faster rate, which preferentially removes low-mass clusters and shifts the turnover of the surviving mass function to higher values. At the same time, the progressive destruction of low-mass clusters narrows the mass distribution, producing the observed decrease in mass-function width at higher density.

An important consequence of this interpretation is that the weak or absent dependence of the turnover mass on Galactocentric distance does not imply that environment is irrelevant. Rather, the turnover mass is more directly linked to internal cluster density than to distance from the Galactic center. Since globular clusters at any given Galactocentric distance exhibit a large scatter in half-mass density, any underlying radial trend is blurred. As a result, the turnover mass can appear nearly insensitive to Galactocentric distance even though it varies significantly with density.

These conclusions are robust to reasonable changes in the assumed form of the evaporation rate. Similar results are obtained when the mass-loss prescription is based on tidal volume density or on surface density rather than half-mass volume density. In each case, the observed structure of the globular cluster mass function can be explained by long-term relaxation-driven evaporation acting on an initially low-mass-rich population. Moreover, the cluster lifetimes required by these models remain within the standard range expected for Milky Way globular clusters, supporting the view that ordinary dynamical evolution is sufficient to account for the main observed features of the present-day mass function.
outputs.L4:
The study investigates the present-day mass function of globular clusters in the Milky Way and how it changes with cluster internal density. Globular clusters are old stellar systems whose masses have been altered over time by dynamical processes, especially two-body relaxation, which gradually drives stars to escape from the cluster. This process, often described as evaporation, reduces cluster masses at a rate that depends on their internal structure and density. By examining the observed Galactic globular cluster population, the study tests whether the characteristic shape of the mass function can be understood as the result of long-term, relaxation-driven mass loss.

A central focus is the turnover mass of the globular cluster mass function, meaning the mass at which the number of clusters peaks before declining toward lower masses. Observationally, the study finds that this turnover mass is not constant across all clusters. Instead, it increases systematically with the half-mass density of clusters: denser clusters tend to have higher turnover masses. This trend is important because it directly links the present-day mass distribution of clusters to their internal dynamical evolution.

To explain this behavior, the study models cluster evolution using mass-loss rates that scale with cluster density. In these models, clusters begin with an initial mass function rich in low-mass objects, similar to the mass functions observed for young cluster systems. Over time, low-mass clusters are preferentially destroyed or depleted, while more massive clusters survive. Because the evaporation rate depends on density, clusters of different densities evolve differently, naturally producing a density-dependent turnover in the mass function.

The study also considers the long-discussed relationship between globular cluster mass function and Galactocentric distance. Previous observations suggested that the turnover mass varies only weakly with distance from the Galactic center, which might appear surprising if the Galactic tidal field were the dominant factor controlling cluster destruction. However, the analysis shows that this weak radial trend can be explained as a secondary consequence of the stronger dependence on cluster density. Since cluster density itself has some correlation with Galactocentric distance, the apparent radial variation in the mass function arises indirectly from the underlying density dependence.

Overall, the results support a picture in which the Milky Way globular cluster system evolved from an initial population containing many low-mass clusters. Over billions of years, slow dynamical evaporation removed a large fraction of these low-mass systems and reshaped the mass function into its present form. The observed increase of turnover mass with half-mass density provides strong evidence that relaxation-driven disruption, with mass-loss rates tied to cluster density, has played a major role in the long-term evolution of Galactic globular clusters.
outputs.L5:
The **Globular Cluster Mass Function (GCMF)** of the **Milky Way** describes how the masses of the Galaxy’s globular clusters are distributed. Globular clusters are dense, ancient systems containing thousands to millions of stars, and they orbit the Milky Way mainly in its halo and bulge. Because they are among the oldest stellar populations in the Galaxy, studying their masses provides important clues about the early formation history of the Milky Way.

In the Milky Way, the GCMF is not a simple power-law distribution. Instead, it shows a characteristic peak, or turnover, at a mass of roughly a few hundred thousand solar masses. This means that globular clusters with intermediate masses are more common, while both very low-mass and very high-mass clusters are less frequent. The low-mass end of the GCMF has likely been strongly shaped by dynamical evolution. Over billions of years, processes such as two-body relaxation, tidal stripping, and shocks from passages through the Galactic disk or near the Galactic center have caused many low-mass clusters to lose stars or dissolve completely.

The present-day GCMF of the Milky Way is therefore different from the initial mass function of globular clusters when they first formed. Astronomers use models of cluster evolution to infer what the original distribution may have looked like. Comparing the Milky Way’s GCMF with those of other galaxies helps researchers understand whether globular cluster formation was universal or influenced by each galaxy’s environment.

Overall, the GCMF is a valuable tool for studying both the long-term dynamical evolution of globular clusters and the assembly history of the Milky Way.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for an astrophysics paper showing that the Milky Way globular cluster mass function depends on half-mass density and can be explained by relaxation-driven evaporation.
counterfactuals.output: We present an analysis of the Galactic globular cluster mass function as a function of internal density, using cluster masses, half-mass radii, and Galactocentric phase-space information for the Milky Way globular cluster system. We find that the shape of the present-day mass function varies systematically with half-mass density: low-density clusters show a turnover at higher mass and a relative depletion of low-mass clusters, while high-density clusters retain a larger fraction of low-mass objects. This trend is difficult to reconcile with a universal, density-independent mass function, but follows naturally from two-body relaxation and the associated evaporation of stars across the tidal boundary. In relaxation-driven evolution, clusters lose mass at a rate set primarily by their half-mass relaxation time, producing stronger fractional mass loss in low-density systems over a Hubble time. We show that a simple evaporation model, applied to an initially broad cluster mass distribution, reproduces both the observed dependence of the mass-function turnover on half-mass density and the approximate invariance of the high-mass slope. The required mass-loss rates are consistent with expectations from standard dynamical evolution in the Galactic tidal field and do not require fine tuning of the initial cluster population. Our results support a picture in which the present-day Milky Way globular cluster mass function is not universal, but is the evolved outcome of density-dependent dynamical erosion. They imply that cluster internal structure must be accounted for when using globular cluster mass functions to infer initial cluster populations, disruption histories, or galaxy formation conditions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main conclusions of a study modeling the Galactic globular cluster mass function with mass-loss rates scaling as \(\mu_{\rm ev} \propto \rho_h^{1/2}\), including implications for turnover mass, density, concentration, and Galactocentric radius.
counterfactuals.output:
A study using evaporation-driven mass loss with

\[
\mu_{\rm ev}\equiv -{dM\over dt}\propto \rho_h^{1/2}
\]

concludes that the present Galactic globular cluster mass function can be understood largely as the result of long-term two-body relaxation acting on an initial cluster mass spectrum, often modeled as a Schechter-like power law with a high-mass cutoff.

Main conclusions:

- **Turnover mass is set by cumulative mass loss.**  
  The peak or turnover mass of the present-day globular cluster mass function is approximately the amount of mass lost over a Hubble time:

  \[
  M_{\rm TO}\sim \mu_{\rm ev} t .
  \]

  Since \(\mu_{\rm ev}\propto \rho_h^{1/2}\), the model predicts

  \[
  M_{\rm TO}\propto \rho_h^{1/2}.
  \]

- **Turnover mass should increase with cluster density.**  
  Denser clusters evaporate faster, so their mass functions are more strongly depleted at low masses and have higher turnover masses. This produces a measurable correlation between \(M_{\rm TO}\) and the present half-mass density \(\rho_h\).

- **The near-universality of the turnover mass is not primordial.**  
  The relatively narrow range of observed globular-cluster turnover masses does not require all clusters to have formed with the same preferred mass. Instead, it can arise dynamically because evaporation removes low-mass clusters and shifts an initially broad, roughly power-law mass function toward a peaked form.

- **Cluster concentration matters mainly as an evolutionary indicator.**  
  Low-concentration clusters are generally more dynamically evolved and closer to disruption, so their mass functions tend to show stronger low-mass depletion. Higher-concentration clusters are typically more massive or dynamically less depleted. However, density is the more direct variable controlling the evaporation rate in this model.

- **Weak dependence on Galactocentric radius.**  
  The model predicts little direct dependence of the turnover mass on Galactocentric radius \(R_{\rm GC}\), except indirectly through any correlation between radius and cluster density. This helps explain why the Galactic globular cluster mass-function turnover is observed to be fairly similar at different radii, despite the much stronger tidal field in the inner Galaxy.

- **Implication for globular-cluster evolution.**  
  The present mass function is mainly shaped by internal relaxation-driven evaporation rather than by a turnover imprinted at birth or by a purely radius-dependent tidal destruction process. The key controlling parameter is the cluster’s internal density, with \(M_{\rm TO}\) scaling roughly as \(\rho_h^{1/2}\), while Galactocentric radius plays a secondary role.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise research-paper conclusion explaining why the apparent universality of the GCMF turnover mass is actually due to cluster evaporation plus scatter in cluster density with Galactocentric distance.
counterfactuals.output:
The apparent universality of the globular-cluster mass-function turnover does not require a universal initial mass scale. Instead, it can arise naturally from long-term dynamical evolution, provided that cluster densities vary substantially at fixed Galactocentric distance. Two-body relaxation drives evaporation, preferentially destroying low-mass clusters and shifting the mass function toward a characteristic turnover mass. In simple models with a single density at each radius, the evaporation rate depends on the tidal field and therefore predicts a strong radial variation in the turnover mass, contrary to observations. However, when the observed scatter in cluster density at a given Galactocentric distance is included, clusters at all radii experience a broad range of evaporation rates. This broadening washes out the otherwise strong radial trend and produces a nearly constant turnover mass across the galaxy.

Thus, the GCMF turnover is best interpreted as an emergent outcome of dynamical evolution rather than as direct evidence for a universal birth mass function. Cluster evaporation sets the mass scale by removing low-mass systems, while the large intrinsic dispersion in cluster densities decouples the turnover from Galactocentric radius. The observed near-invariance of the turnover mass is therefore consistent with environmentally dependent dynamical evolution, once realistic structural diversity among clusters is taken into account.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In technical astronomy language, describe how two-body relaxation and evaporation shape the Milky Way globular cluster mass function, and compare models using half-mass density, tidal density, and tidal surface density.
counterfactuals.output:
Two-body relaxation drives globular clusters (GCs) toward partial energy equipartition and continually scatters stars into the high-energy tail of the distribution function. In a Galactic tidal field, stars with energies above the escape energy leak through the Lagrange points, producing secular “evaporation.” This preferentially destroys low-mass clusters and shifts an initially rising cluster initial mass function toward the observed peaked Milky Way globular-cluster mass function.

A common description is

\[
\frac{dM}{dt}=-\mu_{\rm ev},
\]

with \(\mu_{\rm ev}\) set by some measure of the cluster density and the external tidal field. If \(\mu_{\rm ev}\) is approximately independent of \(M\), an initial power-law or Schechter-like mass function

\[
\psi_0(M)\equiv \frac{dN}{dM}\propto M^{-\beta}\exp(-M/M_c)
\]

evolves to

\[
\psi(M,t)=\psi_0(M+\Delta),
\qquad 
\Delta \equiv \int_0^t \mu_{\rm ev}\,dt ,
\]

so that the low-mass side is depleted and the turnover mass is roughly

\[
M_{\rm TO}\sim \Delta .
\]

Thus the present Galactic GC mass function, with a broad maximum near \(M\sim 10^5\,M_\odot\), can be interpreted as the result of cumulative evaporation over \(\sim 10\)–\(12\) Gyr.

---

## 1. Half-mass-density evaporation model

In the half-mass-density formulation, the evaporation rate is tied to the internal relaxation time at the half-mass radius:

\[
t_{\rm rh}\simeq 
0.138\,\frac{M^{1/2}r_h^{3/2}}
{G^{1/2}\bar m \ln\Lambda},
\]

so that

\[
\mu_{\rm ev}\sim \frac{\zeta M}{t_{\rm rh}}
\propto \rho_h^{1/2},
\]

where

\[
\rho_h \equiv \frac{3M}{8\pi r_h^3}
\]

is the mean density inside the half-mass radius and \(\zeta\sim 0.01\)–\(0.05\) is the dimensionless evaporation efficiency.

Thus,

\[
\frac{dM}{dt}\approx -\mu_{\rm ev}
\approx -\xi\,\rho_h^{1/2},
\]

up to weak dependences on the stellar mass spectrum and Coulomb logarithm.

### Consequences

- Clusters with larger \(\rho_h\) relax faster and lose mass faster per unit time.
- The mass lost over a Hubble time scales as

\[
\Delta M \propto \rho_h^{1/2} t .
\]

- Because the observed Milky Way GC half-mass densities do not vary as strongly with Galactocentric radius as the mean Galactic tidal field does, this model naturally helps explain why the GC mass-function turnover is nearly universal with radius.
- It also explains why low-density clusters are preferentially fragile: they have long crossing times but are more vulnerable to tides and shocks; dense clusters, although internally relaxing faster, can survive strong tidal environments.

This approach is often considered an “internal-density” model: the relaxation physics is evaluated where most of the bound mass resides, near \(r_h\), rather than at the formal tidal boundary.

---

## 2. Tidal-density evaporation model

In a tidal-density model, the relevant density is the mean density associated with the Jacobi or tidal radius,

\[
\rho_t \equiv \frac{3M}{4\pi r_t^3}.
\]

For a cluster on a circular orbit in a host potential,

\[
r_t \simeq 
\left[
\frac{GM}{\Omega^2-\partial^2\Phi/\partial R^2}
\right]^{1/3},
\]

so

\[
\rho_t \sim \frac{\Omega^2}{G}
\]

up to factors depending on the Galactic potential. In an approximately isothermal halo with circular speed \(V_c\),

\[
\Omega = \frac{V_c}{R},
\]

and therefore

\[
\rho_t \propto R^{-2}.
\]

If clusters are tidally filling, \(r_h/r_t\approx\) constant, then

\[
\rho_h \propto \rho_t,
\]

and the evaporation rate becomes

\[
\mu_{\rm ev}\propto \rho_t^{1/2}.
\]

### Consequences

- Clusters in the inner Galaxy experience a larger \(\rho_t\), have smaller tidal radii, shorter relaxation times if tidally filling, and evaporate faster.
- The predicted turnover mass becomes radius-dependent:

\[
M_{\rm TO}(R)\propto \rho_t^{1/2}t
\propto R^{-1}t
\]

for an isothermal potential.
- This tends to predict a stronger radial gradient in the turnover mass than is observed in the Milky Way GC system, unless one invokes orbital eccentricity, pericentric control, mixing, initial radial variations, or underfilling clusters.

The tidal-density model is physically appropriate for Roche-lobe-filling clusters whose half-mass radii scale with their Jacobi radii. It is less successful for underfilling clusters, for which internal structure is decoupled from the instantaneous Galactic tidal boundary.

---

## 3. Tidal-surface-density evaporation model

A third parametrization uses a tidal surface density,

\[
\Sigma_t \equiv \frac{M}{\pi r_t^2},
\]

or equivalently a quantity proportional to \(M/r_t^2\). This lies between a purely internal-density and a purely volume tidal-density description.

Since

\[
r_t\propto \left(\frac{M}{\rho_t}\right)^{1/3},
\]

one has

\[
\Sigma_t \propto \frac{M}{r_t^2}
\propto M^{1/3}\rho_t^{2/3}.
\]

Evaporation laws based on \(\Sigma_t\) therefore introduce an explicit mass dependence even if the underlying escape process is relaxation-driven. Schematically one may write

\[
\mu_{\rm ev}\propto \Sigma_t^\alpha ,
\]

with \(\alpha\) depending on the adopted escape-time prescription. Such models are motivated by the fact that escape is not instantaneous once stars exceed the formal escape energy; the leakage rate depends on both the internal relaxation process and the phase-space structure near the tidal boundary.

### Consequences

- The mass-loss rate is more sensitive to the external tidal field than in a pure half-mass-density model, but less simply tied to \(\rho_t^{1/2}\) than in a Roche-filling tidal-density model.
- Because \(\Sigma_t\propto M^{1/3}\rho_t^{2/3}\), lower-mass clusters at fixed \(\rho_t\) do not all evaporate at exactly the same absolute rate.
- This can produce a somewhat different low-mass shape of the evolved mass function compared with the simple constant-\(\mu_{\rm ev}\) model.
- The predicted radial variation of the turnover is generally intermediate between the weak radial trend of half-mass-density models and the stronger trend of pure tidal-density models.

---

## Comparison of the three prescriptions

| Model | Controlling quantity | Typical evaporation scaling | Physical regime | Main prediction for GC mass function |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Half-mass density | \(\rho_h=3M/8\pi r_h^3\) | \(\mu_{\rm ev}\propto \rho_h^{1/2}\) | Relaxation governed by internal structure near \(r_h\) | Produces a nearly universal turnover if \(\rho_h\) varies weakly with radius |
| Tidal density | \(\rho_t=3M/4\pi r_t^3\sim \Omega^2/G\) | \(\mu_{\rm ev}\propto \rho_t^{1/2}\) for tidally filling clusters | Roche-lobe-filling clusters controlled by Galactic tide | Predicts stronger radial dependence of \(M_{\rm TO}\), especially in inner Galaxy |
| Tidal surface density | \(\Sigma_t=M/\pi r_t^2\) | \(\mu_{\rm ev}\propto \Sigma_t^\alpha\), with model-dependent \(\alpha\) | Intermediate treatment including delayed escape through tidal boundary | Gives intermediate radial and mass dependence |

---

## Implications for the Milky Way GC mass function

The present Milky Way GC mass function is approximately lognormal-like, with a turnover near

\[
M_{\rm TO}\sim 1\text{--}2\times 10^5\,M_\odot,
\]

whereas young massive cluster systems often have power-law mass functions,

\[
\frac{dN}{dM}\propto M^{-2}.
\]

Two-body relaxation plus evaporation transforms an initially rising low-mass distribution into a peaked one by removing low-mass clusters on shorter relaxation timescales. The high-mass end is affected less by evaporation and more by the initial truncation mass, dynamical friction in the inner Galaxy, and possibly early stellar-evolution mass loss.

The half-mass-density prescription is often favored phenomenologically because it reproduces the weak observed dependence of the GC mass-function turnover on Galactocentric radius. Pure tidal-density models tend to overpredict radial variations unless cluster orbits, eccentricities, underfilling, and early evolution are carefully included. Tidal-surface-density models provide a more hybrid description, attempting to capture the fact that evaporation is driven by internal relaxation but regulated by escape through the Galactic tidal boundary.

In short: two-body relaxation supplies stars to the escape region of phase space; the Galactic tidal field defines how easily they are lost; and the adopted density variable—\(\rho_h\), \(\rho_t\), or \(\Sigma_t\)—determines how strongly the evolved globular-cluster mass function depends on internal structure, orbit, and Galactocentric environment.
